facts: Aggersborg, Fyrkat, Nonnebakken, Trelleborg and Borgring were constructed around 970–980 during the reign of Harald Bluetooth.
The fortresses shared a precise geometric design with circular earth-and-turf ramparts, four cardinal gateways and timber-paved axial streets.
Rows of large wooden longhouses were arranged in the quadrants formed by the crossing streets.
The coordinated fortress network demonstrates the centralisation of power under the Danish Jelling Dynasty.
Open agricultural land was a dominant feature of Viking Age Denmark, where farmers cultivated cereals and grains and kept livestock.
Danish villages and farmsteads often occupied territories that had been inhabited and worked for centuries.
Managed mixed woodland, meadows and wetlands remained beside the cultivated lowlands and supplied grazing, timber and fuel.
Longhouses and farmstead sizes varied substantially, providing archaeological evidence of wealth differences within rural communities.
Skuldelev 5 was built in Denmark as a warship around 1030 and later became part of a defensive barrier in Roskilde Fjord.
Viking warships were long, narrow and swift vessels equipped with many oars and a single square sail.
Different Viking ship types were specialised for warfare, long-distance cargo, coastal trade and fishing.
The Skuldelev finds preserve evidence of Danish boat-building practice, fleet organisation and maritime culture.
Danish shipbuilders produced long, narrow warships designed to move warriors efficiently under oars and a single square sail.
Skuldelev 5 was built in Denmark around 1030 using both new and reused timbers.
The Skuldelev ship finds include warships, cargo vessels, coastal traders and smaller fishing or cargo craft.
Coasts, fjords and narrow waterways were essential corridors for communication, trade and military movement in Viking Age Denmark.
